notes.1a: Most candidates recorded the data required correctly, the values recorded suggested they were able to collect the expected volume of carbon dioxide. The number of decimal places used when recording data should be appropriate for the apparatus used. A few candidates were penalised for omitting units from table headings.
notes.1i: Candidates found this question challenging. Many candidates were able to give a correct value for the uncertainty in a single reading but few then went on to use that value in a correct expression. A common error was failing to double the value for a single reading when two readings are required.
notes.1ii: More able candidates were awarded this mark. A common error was the failure to divide the answer to part
notes.1iii: Most candidates scored well on this calculation question.
notes.1d: Most candidates recorded a value for the rough titre although there were some who did not record the relevant burette readings. Marks were also lost by a few candidates because the burette readings for the accurate titrations were only given to one decimal place. Burettes are calibrated at 0.10cm3 so should be read to the nearest 0.05cm3. Candidates should be advised to stop experimenting once they have an accurate titre that is within 0.10cm3 of any other accurate titre. Most candidates were able to gain at least 1 of the 3 marks available.
notes.1e: The mean was generally calculated correctly. A 3 decimal place mean (e.g. 25.275) is no longer accepted.
notes.1iv: Most candidates were familiar with the processing required.
notes.2i: This question was not answered well. Few candidates managed to score all three marks. Where a test or reaction is unfamiliar, candidates should take particular care to note down every observation and to be thorough when testing for gases.
notes.2ii: Many candidates scored one mark here but few candidates scored both marks. Candidates should be advised to note down the starting colour for observations involving a colour change.
notes.2iv: Candidates frequently gave the formula of an ion or the name of an element plus an oxidation state rather than the formula/name of an element required to gain the mark. CHEMISTRY
notes.key_messages: • Candidates who demonstrated a good knowledge of key definitions and applied well-rehearsed arguments to appropriate situations scored more marks. • Candidates who produced vague, imprecise definitions and used details of knowledge with less accuracy and, on occasions, indiscriminately scored lower marks. General comments Candidates are expected to balance all chemical equations.
notes.general_comments: General comments Thirteen questions were found to be more straightforward. Questions 1, 2, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 25, 26, 28, 29, Six questions can be said to have been found to be more difficult. Questions 3, 13, 16, 30, 32 and 34. These questions will now be looked at in greater detail. Comments on specific questions The most commonly chosen incorrect answer was C.
